cues.text: In the town of Middelburg , in the Duchy of Brabant, a noblewoman was known for her devotion and careful spiritual formation of her household staff.
Each Lent, she gathered her entire domestic staff to prepare for Easter through confession and Communion, as she had for years by 1374.
Among her servants that Lent was a man known simply as Jan.
He had not been to confession in many years and approached the sacrament with evident indifference.
Attending Mass and receiving Communion only, it seems, he sought to avoid disappointing his employer rather than act out of any genuine devotion.
As soon as the Host touched Jan's tongue, tradition holds, it transformed into visibly bleeding flesh.
Startled, he removed the particle from his mouth at once, and blood dripped from it onto the cloth covering the communion rail.
This happened in full view of the priest and the assembled household.
The recovered relic was formally investigated, and its public veneration was approved.
It was later divided between two locations: a portion remained at St. Peter's Church in Middelburg.
The other was given, at the request of a confessor to the local archbishop, to the Augustinian Fathers in the university city of Louvain , where it remains to this day.

A 1905 monograph by the historian Joseph Wils, professor at the Catholic University of Louvain, gathered and examined nearly all the surviving contemporary documents and testimonies concerning the miracle.

The relic divided between Middelburg and Louvain remains venerated in both places, a single moment of careless devotion transformed, in the memory the Church has kept, into a sign that reached far beyond the household where it began.
